lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Ah, an audience! Stand there and look grave, and I'll sing you something the Wardens wrote before your grandmothers were born.

options.label: Lark? You taught me every song I know, then vanished. No note, nothing.
What brings a songkeeper to Emberwick?

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Look at you. Still holding a lute like it owes you money.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: I left because the songs were moving, and a songkeeper has to move with them. I should have said goodbye. We're terrible at endings. We always think there's another verse.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Stay close this time. If the songs are right, the Vale is about to need someone who can tell the whole of it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Lark sets one foot on the rim of the well and sings, low and clear, until the square goes quiet.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Seven went over the Greywall high, and seven came home with a fire in the sky. The Wardens kept it and the Wardens sang, and the whole Vale warmed where the hearth-bells rang.
lines.direction: sung softly, a simple folk melody

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: That's the Wardens' Song of the Seven. Seven went, seven came home, a gift and a hearth and everyone happy.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: There's a last verse, too. Nobody has sung it in two hundred years. When a song loses its last verse on purpose, it's usually because the last verse was true.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Songs gather where things are about to happen. A starving town, a goblin on a bridge, an ember going cold under the river. This is the best stage in the Vale.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: And someone I've been following came this way. Never mind who. That's a song for later, somewhere colder.

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Anything else? I take requests. I don't take criticism.

options.label: Sing the Song of the Seven again.
Why are you really in Emberwick?

lines.speaker: lark
lines.text: Go on, then. Do something worth a verse.
